```{r}
#| label: setup
source("functions.R")
baselineRate <- 1
beta <- 1.25
referenceTime <- 1
```

# 1. What population are you sampling from?

This is the dependent machine failure process from the class handout. X_t is the time a machine runs between failure
t − 1 and failure t. The first operating time is Exponential(1). After that, the failure rate depends on the previous
operating time:

$$\lambda_t = \lambda_0 e^{\beta (X_{t-1} - \mu)}, \qquad X_t \mid X_{t-1} \sim \text{Exponential}(\lambda_t),$$

with baseline rate λ₀ = `r baselineRate`, β = `r beta` and reference time μ = `r referenceTime`. A long run (more than 1) raises the next failure rate, so the next
run tends to be short; a short run lowers it, so the next run tends to be long. The handout calls this negative or
compensating dependence.

One "sample of size n" here is the first n operating times of one machine, and its sample mean is that machine's
average operating time. I simulate `r format(num, big.mark = ",")` machines for each n.

The CLT assumptions are not met. The operating times are not independent (each one depends on the previous one), and
they are not identically distributed (X_1 is Exponential(1), but the later ones are not).

```{r}
#| label: onePath
#| fig.width: 10
#| fig.height: 4
set.seed(student_id)
pathN <- 200
failureTime <- numeric(pathN)
failureRate <- numeric(pathN)
failureRate[1] <- baselineRate
failureTime[1] <- rexp(1, rate = failureRate[1])
for (t in 2:pathN) {
  failureRate[t] <- baselineRate * exp(beta * (failureTime[t - 1] - referenceTime))
  failureTime[t] <- rexp(1, rate = failureRate[t])
}
plot(1:pathN, failureTime, type = "h", col = "gray40", xlab = "Failure number t", ylab = "Operating time",
     main = paste0("One machine: first ", pathN, " operating times (seed ", student_id, ")"))
abline(h = referenceTime, col = "firebrick", lty = 2)
```

The tall bars are almost always followed by short ones, which is the compensating dependence.

## Long run behaviour

The operating times do not come from one fixed distribution, so to describe the population I simulated many machines
for a long time and kept the values after the process had settled.

```{r}
#| label: longRun
set.seed(student_id)
chains <- 10000
burnIn <- 1000
keep <- 200
x <- rexp(chains, rate = baselineRate)
kept <- matrix(NA, nrow = chains, ncol = keep)
for (t in 2:(burnIn + keep)) {
  x <- rexp(chains, rate = baselineRate * exp(beta * (x - referenceTime)))
  if (t > burnIn) kept[, t - burnIn] <- x
}
longRunValues <- as.vector(kept)
lagCor <- sapply(1:5, function(k) cor(as.vector(kept[, 1:(keep - k)]), as.vector(kept[, (1 + k):keep])))
longRunSD <- sd(rowMeans(kept)) * sqrt(keep)
longRun <- data.frame(
  quantity = c("mean", "sd", "skewness", "excess kurtosis", "lag 1 correlation", "lag 2 correlation",
               "SD of the mean of 200 values times sqrt(200)"),
  value = c(mean(longRunValues), sd(longRunValues), skewness(longRunValues), exKurtosis(longRunValues),
            lagCor[1], lagCor[2], longRunSD)
)
knitr::kable(longRun, digits = 3)
longRunMean <- mean(longRunValues)
```

In the long run the operating times have mean `r round(longRunMean, 3)`, not 1, and SD `r round(sd(longRunValues), 2)`, not 1. Neighbouring values
are negatively correlated (lag 1: `r round(lagCor[1], 2)`), and the correlation flips sign from lag to lag
(`r paste(round(lagCor, 2), collapse = ", ")` for lags 1 to 5): long, short, long, short. The last row measures how much the mean of many
consecutive values actually varies, in the same units as an SD; I use it in section 2.

# 2. What did you expect before running the simulation?

## What a naive analysis would assume

If I ignored the dependence between the operating times, this would look like an ordinary Exponential(1) problem: the
mean of the sample means would be 1, their SD 1 / sqrt(n), and the shape would pass my standard at about n = 100, as
in 03exponential.qmd. I expected this to be wrong.

## Center

I expected the mean not to stay at 1 but to become clearly larger. An Exponential(1) value is below its mean of 1 with
probability `r round(100 * pexp(1), 0)` percent. In this process a short run lowers the failure rate of the same machine, so its next run
tends to be much longer. Given X_1, the expected next operating time is 1 / λ_2 = e^(−β (X_1 − 1)), and averaging
over X_1 ~ Exponential(1) gives

$$E(X_2) = e^{\beta} \cdot \frac{1}{1 + \beta} = `r round(exp(beta) / (1 + beta), 3)`.$$

```{r}
#| label: checkX2
set.seed(student_id)
x1 <- rexp(1e6, rate = baselineRate)
x2 <- rexp(1e6, rate = baselineRate * exp(beta * (x1 - referenceTime)))
c(simulated = mean(x2), formula = exp(beta) / (1 + beta), standardError = sd(x2) / sqrt(1e6))
```

I checked the formula with one million simulated pairs: the mean of X_2 was `r round(mean(x2), 4)`, within about one standard error
(`r round(sd(x2) / sqrt(1e6), 4)`) of the formula. So I expected the mean of the sample means to be 1 at n = 1 and to move toward the long
run mean of about `r round(longRunMean, 2)` from section 1 as n grows.

## Spread

I expected the SD of the sample means to be clearly larger than the naive SE 1 / sqrt(n). Two effects work in opposite
directions. The zigzag pattern of short, long, short, long (the negative lag 1 correlation) partly cancels out and
makes the average more stable. But the dependence also makes each operating time much more variable: the long run SD
is `r round(sd(longRunValues), 2)`, not 1. I expected this second effect to be much stronger. The last row of the long run table in section 1
measures both effects together: the SD of a long average is about `r round(longRunSD, 2)` / sqrt(n). So I expected the SD of the means to be
about `r round(longRunSD, 1)` times the naive SE for large n.

## Shape

The long run skewness is `r round(skewness(longRunValues), 2)`. If the values were independent, the skewness of the mean would be about
`r round(skewness(longRunValues), 2)` / sqrt(n), which reaches my cutoff of `r criteria$skew` at n = `r predictedN(skewness(longRunValues))`. I could not calculate how the dependence changes
this. The zigzag pattern might help by mixing long and short runs, but my guess was that the shape would become normal
later than n = `r predictedN(skewness(longRunValues))`, because the dependence is one more complication on top of a skewness that already needs about
`r predictedN(skewness(longRunValues))` values.

## n = 30

I expected n = 30 to be far from enough. Even for independent values the skewness at n = 30 would be about
`r round(skewness(longRunValues), 2)` / sqrt(30) = `r round(skewness(longRunValues) / sqrt(30), 2)`, far above my cutoff of `r criteria$skew`.

## Overall

I expected the shape to become normal at some n, later than `r predictedN(skewness(longRunValues))`, but the naive formulas to be wrong at every n: the
center near `r round(longRunMean, 2)` instead of 1, and the spread about `r round(longRunSD, 1)` times the naive SE.

# 3. Which sample sizes did you investigate?

## Coarse grid, then a finer grid

My shape guess was later than n = `r predictedN(skewness(longRunValues))`, so I used a wide grid up to n = 1,000. To simulate 10,000 machines quickly I
used `dependentMeans()` in functions.R, which runs all machines at the same time but uses the same rule as the loop
in section 1.

```{r}
#| label: simulate
coarse <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000)
res <- searchN(NULL, coarse, mu = 1, theoSE = iidSE(1), pred = function(n) c(skew = NA, kurt = NA),
               meansFun = function(n, reps) dependentMeans(n, reps, baselineRate, beta, referenceTime))
tab <- res$table
nStar <- smallestN(tab)
added <- setdiff(tab$n, coarse)
showTable(tab)
```

theoMean and theoSE in this table are the naive values (1 and 1 / sqrt(n)), so seRatio shows how far the naive SE is
off. The finer grid added `r paste(added, collapse = ", ")`.

```{r}
#| label: whichFailed
failTable <- data.frame(
  n = tab$n,
  skewOK = abs(tab$skew) <= criteria$skew,
  kurtOK = abs(tab$exKurt) <= criteria$kurt,
  qqOK = tab$qqCor >= criteria$qqCor
)
knitr::kable(failTable)
skewPass <- smallestN(tab, modifyList(criteria, list(qqCor = 0, kurt = Inf)))
qqPass <- smallestN(tab, modifyList(criteria, list(skew = Inf, kurt = Inf)))
kurtPass <- smallestN(tab, modifyList(criteria, list(skew = Inf, qqCor = 0)))
```

On its own, the skewness check passed from n = `r skewPass`, the kurtosis check from n = `r kurtPass` and the QQ check from n = `r qqPass`.

## How much does the dependence matter?

To see the effect of the dependence directly, I ran the same search with three strengths of dependence. With β = 0
the rate never changes, so the operating times are independent Exponential(1) values, the same population as
03exponential.qmd.

```{r}
#| label: betaCompare
betaValues <- c(0, 0.5, beta)
betaCompare <- do.call(rbind, lapply(betaValues, function(b) {
  r <- searchN(NULL, coarse, mu = 1, theoSE = iidSE(1), pred = function(n) c(skew = NA, kurt = NA),
               meansFun = function(n, reps) dependentMeans(n, reps, baselineRate, b, referenceTime))
  t <- r$table
  data.frame(beta = b,
             chosenN = smallestN(t),
             meanAt1000 = t$simMean[t$n == 1000],
             seRatioAt100 = t$seRatio[t$n == 100],
             skewAt30 = t$skew[t$n == 30])
}))
knitr::kable(betaCompare, digits = 3)
```

With β = 0 the answer is n = `r betaCompare$chosenN[1]`, close to the n = 100 of 03exponential.qmd, the mean stays at 1 and the naive SE is
right. As β grows, the long run mean moves away from 1, the SE ratio changes, and the required n grows. With β = 0.5
the SE ratio is even below 1: the negative dependence wins over the larger SD. With β = `r beta` the larger SD wins.

# 4. When did the sampling distribution become approximately normal?

$$\boxed{n = `r nStar`}$$

```{r}
#| label: summaryNumbers
star     <- tab[tab$n == nStar, ]
lastFail <- tab[tab$n == max(tab$n[tab$n < nStar & !tab$normalEnough]), ]
failed   <- c(skewness = abs(lastFail$skew) > criteria$skew,
              kurtosis = abs(lastFail$exKurt) > criteria$kurt,
              QQ = lastFail$qqCor < criteria$qqCor)
at30     <- tab[tab$n == 30, ]
coverage <- sapply(as.character(tab$n), function(k) {
  m <- res$means[[k]]
  mean(abs(m - longRunMean) <= 1.96 / sqrt(as.numeric(k)))
})
```

The shape became approximately normal at n = `r nStar`, later than `r predictedN(skewness(longRunValues))`, as I guessed. But "normal" here does not mean the naive
CLT is right, so the plot shows the center, the spread and the skewness together.

```{r}
#| label: whyN
#| fig.width: 11
#| fig.height: 4.2
old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
plot(tab$n, tab$simMean, log = "x", pch = 16, ylim = c(0.9, 1.8),
     xlab = "n (log scale)", ylab = "Mean of the sample means", main = "Center")
abline(h = 1, col = "firebrick", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
abline(h = longRunMean, col = "steelblue", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
legend("bottomright", c("Naive: 1", paste("Long run:", round(longRunMean, 2))),
       col = c("firebrick", "steelblue"), lty = 2, lwd = 2, bty = "n")

plot(tab$n, tab$simSD, log = "xy", pch = 16, ylim = range(c(tab$simSD, 1 / sqrt(tab$n), longRunSD / sqrt(tab$n))),
     xlab = "n (log scale)", ylab = "SD of the sample means (log scale)", main = "Spread")
lines(tab$n, 1 / sqrt(tab$n), col = "firebrick", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
lines(tab$n, longRunSD / sqrt(tab$n), col = "steelblue", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("bottomleft", c("Naive: 1 / sqrt(n)", paste0("Long run: ", round(longRunSD, 2), " / sqrt(n)")),
       col = c("firebrick", "steelblue"), lty = 2, lwd = 2, bty = "n")

plot(tab$n, tab$skew, log = "x", pch = ifelse(tab$normalEnough, 16, 4),
     col = ifelse(tab$normalEnough, "steelblue", "firebrick"), lwd = 2,
     xlab = "n (log scale)", ylab = "Skewness of the sample means", main = "Shape")
abline(h = criteria$skew, col = "firebrick", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
abline(v = nStar, col = "steelblue", lty = 3, lwd = 2)
par(old)
```

Left: the center climbs from 1 to about `r round(longRunMean, 2)` and stays there, far from the naive 1. Middle: the simulated SD follows the long
run line, not the naive line. Right: the skewness decides the answer; it drops below `r criteria$skew` and stays there from
n = `r nStar`.

# 5. How do the simulated mean and standard error compare with theory?

```{r}
#| label: seCheck
tab[, c("n", "simMean", "simSD", "theoSE", "seRatio", "seOK")]
```

Center: the simulated mean was `r round(tab$simMean[tab$n == 1], 3)` at n = 1, as expected for one Exponential(1) value, and `r round(tab$simMean[tab$n == 1000], 3)` at n = 1,000,
close to the long run mean `r round(longRunMean, 3)`. The naive mean of 1 is wrong for every n above 1.

Spread: the naive SE check failed at `r sum(!tab$seOK)` of `r nrow(tab)` sample sizes. From n = 10 on, the simulated SD was
`r format(round(min(tab$seRatio[tab$n >= 10]), 2), nsmall = 2)` to `r format(round(max(tab$seRatio[tab$n >= 10]), 2), nsmall = 2)` times the naive SE, close to my prediction of `r round(longRunSD, 2)`.

What this means in practice: if someone used the naive SE to build a 95 percent interval around a machine's average
operating time, the interval would contain the long run mean only `r round(100 * coverage[as.character(nStar)])` percent of the time at n = `r nStar` and
`r round(100 * coverage["1000"])` percent at n = 1,000, instead of 95 percent. More data does not fix this, because the naive interval is too
narrow by about the same factor at every n.

# 6. Why did you choose that value?

The red curve is the normal curve the naive CLT predicts (mean 1, SD 1 / sqrt(n)); the dashed blue curve is a normal
curve with the simulated mean and SD.

```{r}
#| label: samplingPlots
#| fig.width: 11
#| fig.height: 6
plotSampling(res, nShow = unique(c(1, 30, nStar, 1000)), mu = 1, theoSE = iidSE(1), label = "Machine average")
```

At n = 1 the histogram is the Exponential(1) shape, and the red and blue curves are almost the same. At n = 30 the
histogram is still right skewed, and the red naive curve is already in the wrong place: it is a narrow peak near 1 at
the left edge. At n = `r nStar` and n = 1,000 the histogram is bell shaped and follows the blue curve, centered near `r round(longRunMean, 2)`; the red
naive curve, centered at 1 and much narrower, is so far to the left that it falls outside the plotted window. The QQ
plots at these n are close to straight lines: the shape is normal even though the naive center and spread are wrong.

```{r}
#| label: convergence
#| fig.width: 11
#| fig.height: 4
plotConvergence(tab, label = "Dependent")
```

Is n = 30 enough? No: at n = 30 the skewness was `r round(at30$skew, 3)` and the tail shares beyond ±1.96 were
`r round(100 * at30$tailLow, 2)` and `r round(100 * at30$tailHigh, 2)` percent.

I chose n = `r nStar` because:

* At n = `r nStar` the skewness was `r round(star$skew, 3)`, the excess kurtosis `r round(star$exKurt, 3)` and the QQ correlation `r round(star$qqCor, 4)`, all within my
  cutoffs, and every larger n I tested also passed.
* At the largest n that still failed (n = `r lastFail$n`), the check that failed was `r paste(names(failed)[failed], collapse = " and ")` (skewness `r round(lastFail$skew, 3)`).
* This answer is only about the shape. The naive center and spread are wrong at every n, so n = `r nStar` is the n at which
  the mean is normal around the wrong center with the wrong width, if the naive formulas are used.

# 7. What surprised you?

```{r}
#| label: predictionCheck
predictionCheck <- data.frame(
  Prediction = c(
    "Mean starts at 1 at n = 1",
    paste("Mean climbs toward the long run mean of about", round(longRunMean, 2)),
    paste("SD of the means about", round(longRunSD, 1), "times the naive SE"),
    paste("Shape normal later than n =", predictedN(skewness(longRunValues)), "(guess)"),
    "n = 30 not enough",
    "Naive formulas wrong at every n"
  ),
  Result = c(
    paste("Mean at n = 1:", round(tab$simMean[tab$n == 1], 3)),
    paste("Mean at n = 1,000:", round(tab$simMean[tab$n == 1000], 3)),
    paste0("Ratio ", format(round(min(tab$seRatio[tab$n >= 10]), 2), nsmall = 2), " to ", format(round(max(tab$seRatio[tab$n >= 10]), 2), nsmall = 2), " from n = 10"),
    paste("n =", nStar),
    paste("Skewness at n = 30:", round(at30$skew, 3)),
    paste("Naive SE check failed at", sum(!tab$seOK), "of", nrow(tab), "n")
  ),
  Match = c("Same", "Same", "Same",
            ifelse(nStar > predictedN(skewness(longRunValues)), "Same", "Different"), "Same", "Same")
)
knitr::kable(predictionCheck)
```

The biggest surprise was that the shape did become normal, as the general CLT for weakly dependent processes says,
but at the wrong place. A histogram at n = `r nStar` looks perfectly fine, and nothing in its shape warns that the naive
center is off by `r round(100 * (longRunMean - 1))` percent and the naive SE is too small by a factor of about `r round(longRunSD, 1)`. The shape checks I used for every
other population would have passed this one too. Only comparing the center and the spread with theory showed the
problem.

The second surprise was that the direction of the SE error is not fixed. With β = `r beta` the SE was larger than the naive one,
as I predicted, because the larger SD of each value won over the cancelling of neighbours. But in the β comparison in
section 3, with β = 0.5 the cancelling won and the naive SE was even too large. So which effect wins depends on how
strong the dependence is, and I could not have known it without simulating.

The third surprise was how much later the shape became normal. I guessed later than `r predictedN(skewness(longRunValues))`, and the answer was `r nStar`, about
`r round(nStar / predictedN(skewness(longRunValues)), 1)` times that. Two possible reasons are that the early values come from a different distribution than the later
ones, and that the dependence changes how the skewness of a sum adds up. I did not test which one matters more.

## Limitations

* The long run mean, SD and correlations come from a simulation (10,000 machines, 200 kept values each), not from an
  exact formula, so they have some Monte Carlo error.
* Every machine starts from X_1 ~ Exponential(1), so the average of the first n values mixes the start with the long
  run. A machine observed after it has been running for a while would give different results for small n.
* I only used β = `r beta`, λ₀ = 1 and μ = 1 for the main answer; the β comparison shows that the answer depends strongly
  on β.
* The model is a stylized example from the handout, not a real reliability model.
* All rows come from one random stream (seed `r student_id`), so they are not independent of each other.
